bug_semantics: In releases before 1.0.4, PickleScan extracted explicit GLOBAL, INST, and STACK_GLOBAL references and checked those names against a finite unsafe-global blocklist, but it did not interpret the callable/value flow produced by REDUCE. An attacker can therefore encode pkgutil.resolve_name as the only visible global, call it with a data string such as 'os:system' in a first REDUCE to obtain a blocked callable, and invoke that returned callable in a second REDUCE. Because pkgutil.resolve_name was not in the blocklist and the eventual os.system reference never appears as a pickle global, the malicious pickle had issues_count == 0 despite executing arbitrary code when unpickled. The gadget makes every blocklisted target reachable through the same indirection.
flaw_origin: The flaw originates in the first scanner implementation, commit c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e. That commit created src/picklescan/scanner.py with an explicit _suspicious_globals blocklist, _list_globals logic limited to GLOBAL and STACK_GLOBAL, and scan_pickle_bytes logic that increments issues_count only when the extracted module/name is present in that list. pkgutil.resolve_name was neither listed nor semantically followed through REDUCE. This is the smallest repository commit that created the vulnerable security decision; it is not a move, refactor, revert, release-only commit, or squash aggregate.
ai_marker: No AI marker in the BIC commit object. `git cat-file commit c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e` shows author and committer `Matthieu Maitre <mmaitre314@users.noreply.github.com>` and the complete message `Implement Pickle scanner`, with no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, AI trailer, or bot identity.
evidence: First-party advisory https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/security/advisories/GHSA-vvpj-8cmc-gx39 states affected versions `<1.0.4`, patched version `1.0.4`, and documents the exact two-REDUCE chain: visible STACK_GLOBAL pkgutil.resolve_name; resolve_name('os:system') returns os.system; the second REDUCE invokes it while PickleScan reports zero issues.

Run `git show --format=fuller --patch c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e -- src/picklescan/scanner.py setup.cfg` in the validated clone. The commit creates scanner.py from /dev/null. Its _suspicious_globals list omits pkgutil; _list_globals collects only GLOBAL and STACK_GLOBAL; scan_pickle_bytes increments issues_count only for a listed extracted global. The same commit's setup.cfg declares version 0.0.1.

Run `git ls-tree -r --name-only 6a76b8c3ac67dc04181e600614ecf2a423cca326`. The complete parent tree contains only .gitignore, LICENSE, README.md, conda.yaml, requirements.txt, and setup.cfg: no src tree and no scanner or vulnerable blocklist/classification logic. This directly verifies parent absence.

Run `git log --all -S '_suspicious_globals' --patch -- src/picklescan/scanner.py`. Pickaxe reaches c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e as the addition of the blocklist and its fail-open membership check; the later f98f9bd89b16ab1b1b6366acddd1b2a4d36fe9 only renames it to _unsafe_globals while preserving the mechanism. Run `git log -L ':scan_pickle_bytes:src/picklescan/scanner.py' HEAD` as the independent line-history cross-check; it likewise terminates at c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e, where scanner.py is added from /dev/null.

Run `git log --all -S '"pkgutil"' --patch -- src/picklescan/scanner.py tests/init_data_files.py tests/test_scanner.py`. The only scanner blocklist addition is bf26452ae2e3204429762c2bb1aa9eacd40436bb, which adds `"pkgutil": {"resolve_name"}` and a regression assertion that GHSA-vvpj-8cmc-gx39.pkl is Dangerous.

Run `git show --format=fuller --patch bf26452ae2e3204429762c2bb1aa9eacd40436bb`. The single-parent commit `Fix security advisories (#65)` explicitly includes `Fix GHSA-vvpj-8cmc-gx39`, adds pkgutil.resolve_name to _unsafe_globals, adds the advisory fixture and test, and changes setup.cfg from 1.0.3 to 1.0.4. Thus this commit is both the direct code fix and the closing release commit.

Run `git tag --sort=version:refname --format='%(refname:short) %(objectname)'`. It maps v1.0.3 to b9997634683a4f4bd0c7e3701e7ce7e90fe70e8c and v1.0.4 directly to bf26452ae2e3204429762c2bb1aa9eacd40436bb. `git diff v1.0.3 v1.0.4 -- setup.cfg src/picklescan/scanner.py tests/test_scanner.py` shows the exact 1.0.3-to-1.0.4 version bump and pkgutil blocklist/test additions. The earliest tagged descendant is v0.0.2, while the BIC itself declares 0.0.1, so the vulnerable lifecycle begins with the first scanner release and ends at 1.0.4.

Run `git cat-file commit c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e`. The raw BIC object has one parent, human author and committer Matthieu Maitre, and only the subject `Implement Pickle scanner`; there are no trailers or bot/AI identities. AI-related material in the later fix is irrelevant under the BIC-only rule.
reasoning: The advisory mechanism depends on two properties that were introduced together by c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e: only literal pickle globals are extracted, and only names on an explicit blocklist become findings. pkgutil.resolve_name predates this project and was omitted from the new blocklist, so its returned callable crosses a REDUCE boundary the scanner does not model. Direct inspection shows the parent has no scanner at all, while -S and -L independently trace the security mechanism to this non-merge creation commit; later renaming and list growth do not introduce the flaw. The 1.0.4 commit directly closes this gadget by classifying pkgutil.resolve_name as dangerous and adds a matching regression fixture/test, with the tag and setup.cfg establishing the version boundary. The BIC commit object contains only a human identity and ordinary one-line message, with no AI provenance marker. Under the required BIC-only evidence rule, the closed judgment is therefore NOT_AI regardless of any AI-related artifact associated with the 2026 fix.
